lines.text: They expected the bottom of the hole to be about a hundred degrees.
It was about a hundred and eighty.
That's eighty degrees hotter than boiling water.
The plan was fifteen kilometres. The team's own straight-line projection put the rock there at about two hundred and sixty-six degrees.
Going down, rock warms up. Near the top here, about one degree every hundred metres.
By six or seven kilometres, closer to two. The warming itself was speeding up.
And heat doesn't just feel bad. It breaks machines.
So what does rock eighty degrees past boiling do to a drill? The full video shows what broke.
